title: Cohesion and coupling
idea: Cohesion is how closely a class's parts serve one purpose; coupling is how much a class depends on others. Aim for high cohesion and low coupling.
points: A cohesive class has one job, and its methods share its fields.
Coupling grows with every concrete class you construct, call or import.
Depend on narrow interfaces, passed in through the constructor.
Low coupling lets you change or test one class without touching others.

hero.caption: Use these on any class diagram. In the code below, Invoicing has a fan-out of two: the Sender interface and the small PriceBook class.

code.title: Cohesive, loosely coupled
code.caption: Each class has one job. `Invoicing` knows only two small collaborators, both passed in.

walk.text: `Sender` is a one-method interface: all `Invoicing` needs to know about delivery.
`Outbox` is one way to send. Email, SMS or a test fake fit the same slot.
`PriceBook` only knows prices. Changing a price touches this class and nothing else.
Collaborators arrive through the constructor; `Invoicing` never calls `new` on them.
`bill` uses both fields: a small, cohesive method that coordinates and owns no details.
`main` wires the parts together. Swapping `Outbox` needs no edit to `Invoicing`.

pitfalls: Do not split classes into trivial fragments; many chatty pieces raise coupling again.
Do not let two classes share one mutable object; a change ripples to both.
Watch for chains like `a.getB().getC().run()`; they couple you to internals.

quiz.why: `PriceBook` gives 340 for a pad and the default 900 for anything unknown. `Outbox` prefixes the recipient, so the line is `li: total 1240`.

takeaway: One job per class; few, narrow, injected collaborators.
